faq.a: Acute appendicitis is the most common cause of acute abdomen requiring surgery in young adults. However, in women, gynaecological causes like ectopic pregnancy or pelvic inflammatory disease must also be considered.
faq.q: What is the most common cause of acute abdomen in young adults?

faq.a: Suspect a strangulated hernia when an incarcerated (irreducible) hernia becomes painful, tender, and is associated with signs of systemic toxicity like fever, tachycardia, or peritonism over the hernia site. This is a surgical emergency.
faq.q: When should I suspect a strangulated hernia?

faq.a: Initial steps include ABC stabilization, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, analgesia, nasogastric tube insertion for decompression, and urgent surgical consultation for laparotomy and repair of the perforation.

exam: A 30-year-old male presents with sudden onset severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with vomiting. On examination, he has tenderness in the epigastrium and guarding. What is your immediate differential diagnosis and what single investigation would you prioritize if only basic labs and X-rays are available? — Suspect acute pancreatitis or perforated peptic ulcer. You are on a ward round in a rural hospital with limited resources. A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of right iliac fossa pain, fever, and vomiting. She has localized guarding and rebound tenderness. An ultrasound is unavailable. How would you proceed with diagnosis and initial management? — Clinical diagnosis of acute appendicitis is highly likely. Initial management includes IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesia, and urgent surgical consultation.

A patient with a known inguinal hernia presents with a painful, irreducible lump in the groin, associated with abdominal distension and vomiting. What is the most critical complication to rule out, and what physical sign would strongly suggest it? — The most critical complication is strangulation. Strong suggestion would be tenderness over the hernia sac, erythema of the overlying skin, and signs of systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia).

Describe the key differences in presentation between a small bowel obstruction and a large bowel obstruction. — Small bowel obstruction typically presents with colicky abdominal pain, early and profuse vomiting (often bilious, then faeculent), distension that is less pronounced, and constipation that may be late. Large bowel obstruction presents with more gradual onset, less prominent vomiting (often late), marked abdominal distension, and absolute constipation.

A patient is post-operative day 3 following an appendectomy. They develop fever, increasing abdominal pain, and purulent discharge from the wound. What are your immediate concerns and how would you manage this? — Immediate concerns are wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess, or anastomotic leak (if applicable). ai.title: General Surgical Principles and Common Conditions
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: General Surgery encompasses a broad range of conditions requiring surgical intervention, primarily focusing on the abdomen, skin, breast, and endocrine system. This study page emphasizes clinical reasoning for common surgical presentations in low-resource settings. It covers diagnosis, management, and potential pitfalls.

b: A surgical diagnosis is often a clinical diagnosis, supported by investigations.
Prioritize life-threatening conditions and those requiring urgent intervention.
sections.p: General Surgery is a surgical specialty that focuses on the abdominal contents (esophagus, stomach, small bowel, colon, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts, and often the spleen and thyroid gland), breast, skin, and soft tissues. Diagnosis relies heavily on a thorough history, physical examination, and judicious use of available investigations, especially in resource-limited settings.

b: Assess for signs of sepsis: fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, altered mental status.
Evaluate organ perfusion: urine output, capillary refill time, blood pressure.
Consider the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification for surgical risk assessment.
sections.p: Severity assessment in general surgery often involves evaluating the patient's physiological stability, the extent of organ dysfunction, and the local progression of the disease. Staging systems are specific to individual conditions (e.g., cancer staging) but general principles apply to acute surgical emergencies.

b: Acute abdomen: Appendicitis, perforated peptic ulcer, intestinal obstruction (adhesions, hernia, volvulus), typhoid perforation, ectopic pregnancy.
Hernias: Inguinal, umbilical, incisional – often presenting with complications like obstruction or strangulation.
Trauma: Blunt or penetrating abdominal injuries, often from road traffic accidents or interpersonal violence.
Breast lumps: Fibroadenoma, breast abscess, breast cancer (often presenting at advanced stages).
Thyroid swellings: Goitre (endemic or multinodular), thyroiditis, thyroid cancer.
Anorectal conditions: Haemorrhoids, anal fissures, perianal abscesses, fistulas.
sections.p: Common surgical conditions in East Africa and low-resource settings often include infections, trauma, and neglected chronic conditions. Access to timely care can influence the presentation and severity of these conditions.

b: Abdominal pain: Character, location, radiation, onset, duration, aggravating/relieving factors, associated symptoms.
Swelling/mass: Location, size, consistency, tenderness, reducibility (for hernias), pulsatility.
Vomiting: Character (bilious, faeculent), frequency, associated with pain.
Changes in bowel habits: Constipation, diarrhoea, melena, haematochezia.
Fever: Suggests infection or inflammation.
Weight loss: May indicate malignancy or chronic infection (e.g., TB).
sections.p: Clinical presentation varies widely depending on the condition but often involves pain, swelling, changes in bowel habits, or constitutional symptoms. A systematic approach to history taking and physical examination is crucial.

Investigations should be guided by clinical suspicion and availability. In low-resource settings, basic laboratory tests and imaging are often the first line, with advanced imaging reserved for specific indications or when available.

t.b: Identifies infection (leukocytosis), anaemia (blood loss, chronic disease), or thrombocytopenia (coagulopathy). Elevated white cell count suggests inflammation/infection.
Assesses hydration status, renal function, and electrolyte imbalances (e.g., in vomiting, diarrhoea, obstruction). Derangements can indicate severity or guide fluid resuscitation.
Evaluates liver and biliary tree function (e.g., in jaundice, cholangitis, liver masses). Elevated bilirubin, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT can point to specific pathologies.
Diagnoses pancreatitis. Significantly elevated levels (3 times upper limit of normal) are indicative.
Screens for urinary tract infection, haematuria, or proteinuria, which can mimic abdominal pathology.
Essential for patients who may require blood transfusion (e.g., trauma, GI bleed, major surgery). If unavailable, O negative blood may be used in emergencies.
Detects free air under the diaphragm (perforation), dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels (obstruction), or foreign bodies. Limited sensitivity but often readily available.

Checks for free air under the diaphragm (perforation), pneumonia (can cause referred abdominal pain), or pleural effusions. If erect CXR is not possible, a left lateral decubitus AXR can show free air.

Visualizes solid organs (liver, spleen, kidneys), gallbladder, appendix, and can detect free fluid, abscesses, or masses. Operator-dependent but often available and non-invasive. Useful for acute cholecystitis, appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, ascites.

Provides detailed imaging of abdominal organs, vasculature, and pathology. Gold standard for many acute abdominal conditions, trauma, and cancer staging. If unavailable, clinical judgment and other imaging modalities are paramount.

b: Peritonism (guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness): Suggests peritonitis, often due to perforation or severe inflammation.
Haemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia): Indicates shock (hypovolaemic, septic), often from bleeding or severe infection.
Altered mental status: Sign of severe sepsis, hypovolaemia, or metabolic derangement.
Absent bowel sounds with abdominal distension: Suggests paralytic ileus or late-stage obstruction.
Scrotal/inguinal swelling with pain and irreducibility: Suggests incarcerated or strangulated hernia.
Progressive jaundice with pale stools and dark urine: May indicate biliary obstruction, potentially malignant.
Rapidly enlarging painful breast lump with skin changes: Highly suspicious for inflammatory breast cancer or abscess.
sections.p: Recognizing red flags is critical for timely intervention and preventing severe complications. These often indicate life-threatening conditions requiring immediate surgical consultation.

b: Resuscitation: Airway, Breathing, Circulation (ABC) assessment and management. IV fluids for hypovolaemia, oxygen for hypoxia.
Pain control: Administer analgesia early, often parenteral, while monitoring for masking of signs.
Antibiotics: Broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected infection (e.g., peritonitis, appendicitis, cholangitis). Choose agents effective against common local pathogens.
Nasogastric tube insertion: For bowel obstruction or severe vomiting to decompress the stomach.
Urinary catheter insertion: To monitor urine output and assess renal perfusion.
Surgical intervention: Definitive treatment for most surgical conditions (e.g., appendectomy, laparotomy for perforation, hernia repair, tumour excision).
Nutritional support: Especially for prolonged illness or post-operative recovery.
sections.p: Management in general surgery involves resuscitation, diagnosis, and definitive surgical intervention when indicated. Prioritize stabilization of the patient before surgery. In low-resource settings, conservative management may be considered for some conditions if surgical facilities are limited, but with careful monitoring.

b: Wound care: Regular dressing changes, monitoring for signs of infection (redness, swelling, discharge, pain).
Pain management: Oral analgesia as needed, weaning from parenteral.
Mobilization: Early ambulation to prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary complications.
Diet progression: Gradual reintroduction of oral intake as tolerated.
Patient education: On symptoms of complications, medication adherence, and lifestyle modifications.
Prevention: Vaccination (e.g., tetanus), safe water and food practices, early treatment of infections, screening for certain cancers (e.g., breast self-examination).
sections.p: Post-operative care, wound management, and patient education are crucial for good outcomes. Prevention strategies include vaccination, hygiene, and early presentation for symptoms.

b: Acute appendicitis vs. mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, urinary tract infection, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy.
Biliary colic vs. acute pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, myocardial infarction.
Intestinal obstruction vs. paralytic ileus, severe gastroenteritis.
Perforated peptic ulcer vs. acute pancreatitis, myocardial infarction, renal colic.
Abdominal wall haematoma vs. incarcerated hernia, abscess.
sections.p: Many medical conditions can mimic surgical emergencies, leading to diagnostic challenges. Careful differentiation is essential to avoid unnecessary surgery or delayed medical treatment.

b: Normal white blood cell count: Does not rule out appendicitis or other infections, especially in immunocompromised patients or early stages.
Negative abdominal X-ray: Does not exclude perforation or obstruction, particularly small perforations or early obstructions.
Normal amylase/lipase: Can occur in pancreatitis due to alcohol or chronic disease, or if presentation is delayed.
Negative ultrasound: Operator-dependent; a negative scan for appendicitis or cholecystitis does not completely rule out the diagnosis if clinical suspicion is high.
Referred pain: Pain from thoracic or genitourinary conditions can present as abdominal pain, leading to misdiagnosis if not considered.
sections.p: Interpreting investigations requires clinical correlation, especially when resources are limited or patient factors complicate results. A single test result should not override strong clinical suspicion.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden, severe abdominal pain that worsens rapidly
Abdominal distension with inability to pass flatus or stool
Persistent vomiting, especially if bilious or faeculent
Fever with chills and severe abdominal pain
Any signs of shock: confusion, rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, cold clammy skin
Unexplained vaginal bleeding with severe abdominal pain in women of childbearing age
Irreducible, painful lump in the groin or umbilical area
